title: Food Irradiation
lead: Ionizing radiation is used to treat food against pests, spoilage and the microorganisms that cause illness. This section describes the radiation and the doses food irradiation uses, asks whether irradiated food becomes radioactive, and follows the free radicals that the radiation makes in food and in the organisms it is meant to kill.
objectives: Define food irradiation low dose, and free radicals.
summary_html:
• Food irradiation is the treatment of food with ionizing radiation.
  • Irradiating food can destroy insects and bacteria by creating free radicals and radiolytic products that can break apart cell membranes.
  • Food irradiation has produced no observable negative short-term effects for humans, but its long-term effects are unknown.

figures.original_caption: A food irradiation plant has a conveyor system to pass items through an intense radiation field behind thick shielding walls. The $\gamma$ source is lowered into a deep pool of water for safe storage when not in use. Exposure times of up to an hour expose food to doses up to ${10}^{4}\;\text{Gy}$.

exercises.prompt: Does food irradiation leave the food radioactive? To what extent is the food altered chemically for low and high doses in food irradiation?

answer.solution: No, irradiation does not leave the food radioactive. The $\gamma$ rays, x-rays and electrons used to treat food induce no nuclear reactions, so no nucleus in the food is changed and no radioactivity is left behind. The changes are chemical: ionization breaks molecules and makes free radicals, which react into radiolytic products. At a low dose, up to 1000 Gy, these compounds are made in amounts too small to measure, and spices and many fruits and vegetables show no loss of taste or food value. At a high dose the changes can be measured: about 15% of the nutrients and 25% of the vitamins are lost and the taste changes, losses like those of freezing and cooking.

exercises.prompt: Compare a low dose of radiation to a human with a low dose of radiation used in food treatment.

answer.solution: A low dose in food irradiation is about ten thousand times a low dose to a person. A low dose to a person is less than 100 mSv, which for $\gamma$ rays is less than 0.1 Gy. A low dose in food irradiation is up to 1000 Gy, far above the 4.5 Sv that kills half of the people who receive it. The two are called low for different reasons: one is low for a person, the other is the least that stops the growth of many microorganisms, which are simpler organisms and tolerate much more radiation than people do.

exercises.prompt: Suppose one food irradiation plant uses a ${}^{137}\text{Cs}$ source while another uses an equal activity of ${}^{60}\text{Co}$. Assuming equal fractions of the $\gamma$ rays from the sources are absorbed, why is more time needed to get the same dose using the ${}^{137}\text{Cs}$ source?

answer.solution: The ${}^{137}\text{Cs}$ source deposits less energy in the food each second, so it takes longer to build up the same dose, which is the energy absorbed per kilogram. Equal activities mean equal numbers of decays per second, and equal fractions of the $\gamma$ rays are absorbed, so the difference lies in the energy each decay sends out as $\gamma$ rays. A ${}^{137}\text{Cs}$ decay gives at most one 0.67-MeV $\gamma$ ray, while a ${}^{60}\text{Co}$ decay gives two, averaging 1.25 MeV, about 2.5 MeV in all. The cobalt source therefore deposits roughly four times the energy per second, and the cesium source needs roughly four times as long for the same dose.

exercises.prompt: In the 1980s, the term picowave was used to describe food irradiation in order to overcome public resistance by playing on the well-known safety of microwave radiation. Find the energy in MeV of a photon having a wavelength of a picometer.

answer.hint: Use $\kE = hc/\lambda$ with $hc = 1240\;\text{eV}\cdot\text{nm}$, writing 1 pm as $10^{-3}\;\text{nm}$.
